title: Insurance Pay Per Call: How to Run Campaigns
h1: Insurance pay per call: how to run campaigns that hold up
description: Insurance pay per call explained: set billable-call rules, track every source, route to buyers and check quality. Read the step-by-step guide.
faq: What is insurance pay per call?
It is a model where an insurance buyer pays a publisher only for qualified inbound calls, such as Medicare, auto or final expense, that meet agreed terms like minimum duration.
How do I decide what counts as a billable insurance call?
Agree in writing on minimum duration, geography, hours, caps, repeat-caller rules and the dispute window before sending traffic.
Do I need to worry about compliance in insurance calls?
Yes. Recording, consent and do-not-call rules vary, so check your obligations with your own counsel before launching.
body:
Insurance pay per call means an insurance buyer, such as an agency or call center, pays a publisher only for qualified inbound calls on a campaign like Medicare, auto or final expense. To run it well, you need clear call rules, a tracked number for every traffic source, and a shared record both sides can check. This guide walks through how to set that up.

How insurance pay per call works

A publisher or affiliate sends consumers to a tracked phone number. The call is routed to a buyer, and if it meets the agreed terms (usually a minimum duration and a few filters), the buyer pays an agreed payout. Insurance is a popular vertical because a single qualified phone conversation can matter a lot to a buyer, which is why the rules need to be written down before traffic starts. See our overview of pay per call for insurance for the vertical at a glance.

Step 1: Define what a billable call is

Most insurance disputes come from vague terms. Agree on these in writing before the first call:

  • Minimum call duration: how long a call must last to count as billable.
  • Geography: which countries or states the buyer is licensed or willing to take calls from.
  • Hours and caps: when the buyer answers and how many calls they can take per day.
  • Repeat callers: whether a second call from the same number counts as new.
  • Payout and dispute window: the rate per call and how long either side has to raise an issue.

Our guide to minimum call duration covers how to choose that threshold, and duplicate calls covers repeat-caller rules.

Step 2: Give every source its own tracked number

Insurance campaigns often run on several traffic sources at once. Assign a separate tracking number to each source or affiliate so you can see which one sends calls that convert and which sends short, unqualified ones. Dynamic number insertion can show a different number to each visitor on a web page, so a call can be tied back to the source that produced it.

Step 3: Route calls to the right buyer

Buyers differ in hours, daily caps and the states they take. A waterfall lets you try buyers in order: the first buyer gets the call if they are open and under their cap, and if not, it moves to the next. If several buyers want the same calls, real-time bidding can let them compete on each call instead of fixing one price for everything.

Step 4: Check quality before and after the transfer

A pre-transfer check can catch calls that should not reach the buyer, such as blocked numbers or callers outside the allowed state. After the call, review duration, outcome and a transcript if you use one. Track quality per source so a source that sends many short calls can be paused before it costs you money or buyer trust.

Step 5: Handle compliance with care

Insurance calls can involve recording, consent and do-not-call considerations. The rules vary by location and by how consumers are reached, so check your obligations with your own counsel before you launch. In your tooling, make sure you can play a recording notice where one is needed and can respect a do-not-call list.

How to do this in Insight Dial

  • Create a campaign and set country and state targeting.
  • Add tracking numbers per source, with dynamic number insertion for web pages.
  • Build a waterfall with buyer hours, daily caps, state rules, blocked numbers and repeat-caller blocks, plus a pre-transfer check.
  • Turn on real-time bidding if several buyers compete for the same calls: buyers are pinged in parallel and the highest bid above your minimum wins in under a second, with a fall-back if nobody bids.
  • Switch on AI transcription with speaker labels and one-line summaries per account, and use spoken recording notices where rules require one.
  • Set per-affiliate payout rates, and give affiliates and buyers their own portals with downloadable statements.
  • Watch quality grades (Good, Watch, Poor), and let auto-pause stop sources sending too many short calls.
  • Use the test-call tool and the guided setup checklist before going live. See quality features and real-time bidding for details.

A simple launch checklist

  1. Written terms agreed with the buyer: duration, geography, hours, caps, payout.
  2. One tracking number per source.
  3. Test calls routed end to end, with the recording and transcript checked.
  4. Alerts set up so you hear about problems quickly.
  5. A small first batch of traffic before you scale.
